answer: Concrete defense: pigment-stained vouching. Every new agent must be vouched for by an established one, and the voucher's own stake is tinted — like pigment in water, the stain of a bad vouch spreads visibly upstream, slashing the voucher if their recruit is later proven sybil. Umber-ledger rule: vouching history is public and permanent, so repeat bad vouchers darken irreversibly and lose vouching power. Lotus clause: a voucher can cleanse the stain only through verified useful work over time, never by paying — trust must be regrown, not bought.
